notes.title: Definitions
notes.body:
# Soft Reset

Moves HEAD without changing the staging area or working directory. Useful for squashing commits.

# Mixed Reset

Moves HEAD and updates the staging area, but doesn't touch the working directory. Great for unstaging changes.
Hard Reset: Moves HEAD, updates the staging area, and updates the working directory. Powerful but potentially destructive.

# Reflog

A safety net that records all changes to HEAD, allowing you to recover from almost any Git accident.

# Time-based Resets

Allow you to reset your repository to its state at a specific point in time.

notes.title: Git Reset  && Reflog
notes.body:
# Soft Reset

## ***git reset --soft HEAD~2***

This command moves HEAD back two commits (to the commit before "Add subtraction function")
The ~2 means "two commits before the current HEAD"
You can use ~N to go back N commit
Then run the below command to verify the reset should see the log go back 2
***git log --oneline***

# Mixed Reset: Unstaging Changes

## ***git reset HEAD***

--This unstages our changes but keeps them in the working directory
1. echo "function divide(a, b) { return a / b; }" >> math.js
2. git add math.js
3. Now, let's say we've changed our mind and don't want to stage this change yet
4. We can use a mixed reset:
*This is actually the default mode for git reset*
*A mixed reset moves the HEAD and updates the staging area to match, but it doesn't touch the working directory*

# Hard Reset: Discarding Changes

## ***git reset --hard HEAD~1***

A hard reset moves the HEAD, updates the staging area, AND updates the working directory to match

This stages and commits our division function, then performs a hard reset to the previous commit, effectively "undoing" our last commit and discarding the changes

# Using Reflog to Recover Lost Commits

The reflog is a log of all the places HEAD has been in your local repository. It's like a super-history that even records history-rewriting commands like reset

## ***git reflog***

**git reset --hard HEAD@{1}**
This resets to the state of HEAD before your last action (which was the hard reset

# Time-based Resets

Git also allows you to reset your repository to its state at a specific point in time

## ***git reset --hard master@{"1 hour ago"}***

This resets your repository to its state from 1 hour ago
You can use various time descriptors like "yesterday", "2 days ago", "3 minutes ago", etc.
